nodes.claim: Establishes the pointwise limit and shows that any possible uniform limit must be this function.
nodes.text: For every $x\in[0,1)$, $x^n\to0$, while $f_n(1)=1$ for every $n$. Thus $(f_n)$ converges pointwise to the function $f$ defined by $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$ and $f(1)=1$. Any uniform limit would also be a pointwise limit, so it would necessarily equal this $f$.

nodes.claim: Claims nonuniform convergence by choosing, for each positive integer $N$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$, the point $x=\varepsilon^{1/N}$. The calculation requires the unstated pointwise limit $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$; fixing one such $\varepsilon$, for example $1/2$, would then match the negation of uniform convergence.
nodes.text: The sequence $\left(f_n\right)_n$ does not converge uniformly, since given $0<\varepsilon<1$ and $N \in \mathbb{Z}_{+}$, for $x=\varepsilon^{1 / N}$ we have $d\left(f_N(x), f(x)\right)=\varepsilon$.

nodes.claim: Offers a second argument based on a cited theorem that allegedly makes continuity of the limit necessary for uniform convergence. Its applicability cannot be checked because Theorem 21.6 is not stated, $f$ is undefined, and the discontinuity of $f$ is not established in the proof.
nodes.text: We can also apply Theorem 21.6: the convergence is not uniform since $f$ is not continuous.
